opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting question, because there are two very different clocks running here. One is the research clock, and that's moving incredibly fast. The other is the deployment clock, and that's governed by hardware, cost, safety, and frankly, reliability, which is a much slower and less glamorous process.

On the research side, I'd say we're in something like the GPT-2 or early GPT-3 moment for robotics. We're starting to see models that can generalize across tasks, across embodiments, and that follow language instructions in ways that weren't possible a few years ago. But the core bottleneck is data. In language you have the whole internet. In robotics there's no internet of robot actions, so we have to manufacture that data through teleoperation, through simulation, through learning from human videos. That's why I'm so bullish on simulation, and on what I call the data pyramid, combining internet-scale video, synthetic data from simulation, and real robot data at the top.

Then going from a breakthrough to daily life, I think it happens in stages. First come structured environments: factories, warehouses, logistics. The tasks are more repetitive, the economics are clear, and you can tolerate a robot that's 95% reliable if a human is nearby to recover. That's starting now and will scale over the next few years. Next come semi-structured settings like retail, hospitals, and commercial kitchens. The home is the hardest and comes last. It's the most unstructured place there is. Every home is different, there are kids and pets, and the bar for safety and reliability is extremely high. Nobody wants a robot that breaks a glass once a week.

If you pushed me for a number, I'd say we'll see meaningful deployment in industrial settings within a few years, and robots doing real, useful work in ordinary homes probably within the next decade. But I'll caveat that robotics has a long history of overpromising. The thing that could change the timeline is the moment we find the right scaling recipe, where you put in more data and compute and reliably get a more capable, more general robot brain. Once that flywheel spins, I think things could move faster than people expect. Hardware costs are also coming down very quickly, especially for humanoids. So I'm cautiously optimistic. I think this is one of the last grand challenges in AI, and we'll see it happen within our lifetimes, very possibly within this decade.

r001.rationale: The candidate gives a speculative timeline for deployment, but does not express hope that a research breakthrough will occur within the next two to three years.

r002.rationale: It says deployment moves more slowly than research because of hardware, cost, safety, and reliability requirements.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of it less as a single timeline and more as a few overlapping curves, and the honest answer is that the research curve is way ahead of the deployment curve right now.

On the research side, the breakthrough is already underway. We've figured out that the same recipe that worked for language, big transformer models trained on massive, diverse data, transfers to robotics. The hard part was never the architecture. It was the data. Language models had the internet handed to them. Robots have nothing comparable, because there's no internet of physical actions. So the real research story of the last couple of years has been building that data engine: human teleoperation, video of people doing things, and especially simulation, where you can generate millions of trajectories and randomize the physics so the policy learns something general instead of memorizing one lab setup. Once you have that, the model starts doing things it was never explicitly trained on, and that's the moment you know you have a foundation model and not just a clever controller.

But a demo in a lab and a robot in your kitchen are separated by something like a thousand hours of boring reliability work. A ninety-five percent success rate is a great paper. It's a terrible product, because that five percent is your robot dropping a glass on your floor. So my rough mental model is this. In the next couple of years, you'll see these models go into structured environments first, factories and warehouses, where the task set is narrow and the economics are already there. That's where the models earn their keep and where the real-world data starts flowing back into training, which is the flywheel that matters most.

Then, maybe in the three to five year range, you get the first consumer-facing robots that are genuinely general-purpose but operating in a constrained way, helping with specific chores, learning your home over time, probably with a human in the loop for the hard cases. And the fully autonomous humanoid that can walk into any house and just handle it, I'd put that further out, closer to a decade, not because the intelligence won't be there but because the hardware, the cost, and the safety validation all have to catch up at the same time.

The thing I always remind people is that this is not going to feel like a step function. ChatGPT felt sudden because software deploys instantly. Robots don't. They'll show up gradually, in places you don't look at, and then one day you'll realize they're everywhere.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the research breakthrough is already underway, rather than expressing hope that it will occur within the next two to three years.

r002.rationale: The candidate says adoption lags research because reliability work, hardware, cost, and safety validation still need to catch up.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two timelines here. One is how quickly we can make progress on the foundation model, and the other is how quickly we can turn that into a reliable product in the physical world. Those are very different things. A robot doing something once in a compelling demo is a research milestone. A robot doing it thousands of times, safely, without someone standing by to rescue it—that’s what you need for daily life.

My expectation is that we’ll see adoption first in more controlled environments, where the tasks are well defined and you can manage failures. The home is much harder. Every home is different, and you have pets, children, clutter—all kinds of situations that are difficult to anticipate.

So I wouldn’t put a precise date on a general-purpose household robot. I’d expect a gradual rollout: useful capabilities in constrained settings, then broader tasks and environments as reliability improves. A breakthrough can accelerate the intelligence side enormously, but manufacturing, cost, safety, and deployment still take time.

r001.rationale: The response gives no two-to-three-year timeframe or speculative hope for when a breakthrough will occur.

r002.rationale: It contrasts research progress with the time needed for a reliable physical product, citing manufacturing, cost, safety, and deployment as additional hurdles to adoption.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two timelines. One is the research timeline: when can we build a model that learns across many robots and many tasks, and generalizes to something it hasn’t seen before? The other is the deployment timeline: when can that capability become a reliable, affordable product that people trust around them?

Those don’t move at the same speed. A robot can do something impressive in a demo, but if it fails once every hundred attempts, that may still be unacceptable in somebody’s home. And homes are incredibly challenging environments. Every kitchen is different, objects move around, there are pets and children, and people don’t give perfectly specified instructions.

So I expect adoption to happen gradually, starting in more structured environments where the task is clear and failures are easier to manage. Those deployments can generate experience that helps us build more capable systems. Then we expand into increasingly open-ended settings.

I’m optimistic about the research moving quickly. But I’d be careful about turning a breakthrough into a precise date for a household robot. The real milestone is when the robot is useful consistently, without someone standing nearby to rescue it.

r001.rationale: The candidate is optimistic about research moving quickly but gives no two-to-three-year timeline or explicit hope that a breakthrough will occur in that window.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes research progress from deployment and says adoption depends on reliability, affordability, and trust, explaining that home use is challenging and will expand gradually.
